title: Phylogenetic Relationships Among Denisovans, Neanderthals, and Modern Humans: The Uniparental Genetic Alternative
content: The whole genome-based tree topology of the modern human-Neanderthal-Denisovan triad situate Neanderthals and Denisovans as sister clades and modern humans as the outgroup. In contrast, the mtDNA and NRY phylogenies support modern humans and Neanderthals as the closest groups. To explain the reasons of this discrepance in favor of the genome-wide phylogeny, several putative introgression phenomena have been proposed, as that of admixture between a very divergent archaic population and the Denisovans that resulted in total substitution of both Denisovan uniparental markers by the archaic ones without the Denisovan nuclear genetic background being affected by that archaic uniparental introgression, and/or that of the admixture between Neanderthals, after its separation from Denisovans, and a population of early modern humans, resulting in a population that retained the uniparental markers of the early modern humans but introgressed the nuclear genome of the early Neanderthals. However, when strong sex-bias is invoked to substitute one of the uniparental markers we have, concomitantly, impeding the fixation of the other sex marker. Furthermore, the massive introduction of the nuclear genome of one group into other group cannot occur without the simultaneous massive introduction of at least one of its uniparental markers. Here we demonstrate that all these difficulties disappear if we accept that the phylogeny deduced from the mtDNA and NRY lineages is the true one and attribute the nuclear topology as the result of population structure, incomplete lineage sorting, and secondary introgression affecting each group differently. The genetic affinities recently found between derived Erectus populations and Denisovans in eastern Asia territories that, at that time, were not occupied by Neanderthals or early modern humans and, the growing possibility that modern humans and Neanderthals shared a common ancestor in northern Africa, an area without any clue of Denisovan presence, also support the genetic tree topology deduced from uniparental markers.
